chief_complaint: rapidly rising creatinine and oliguria in patient with liver cirrhosis and ascites
hpi_details: 57M with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presenting with progressive oliguria and doubling of creatinine unresponsive to albumin and fluid challenges.
ideas: He thinks the heavy fluid accumulating in his abdomen is pressing against his bladder and mechanically blocking his urine from coming out.
concerns: He is worried that his liver has completely failed and that he will not survive long enough to attend his daughter's wedding next month.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will drain the fluid from his belly with a needle so the pressure comes off and he can pass urine again.

available_results.test: Serum creatinine after albumin challenge and diuretic withdrawal
available_results.note: Baseline creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL; there was no improvement after 2 days of IV albumin.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hepatorenal Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes a trial of IV albumin plus vasoconstrictor therapy to improve renal perfusion after excluding other causes of AKI, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: rapidly rising creatinine and oliguria in patient with liver cirrhosis and ascites
Key HPI features: 57M with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presenting with progressive oliguria and doubling of creatinine unresponsive to albumin and fluid challenges.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 92/58, HR 98, Temp 37.0C. Tense ascites, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, scleral icterus, mild asterixis. Bloods: Creatinine doubled from baseline 0.9 to 2.8 mg/dL despite 2 days of IV albumin 1 g/kg/day and diuretic withdrawal; Bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, INR 2.1, Albumin 2.4 g/dL. Urine sodium <10 mEq/L; urinalysis bland with no significant proteinuria, hematuria, or casts. Diagnostic paracentesis excludes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hepatorenal Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Prerenal AKI from volume depletion (would respond to fluids) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever, abdominal pain) — a common trigger that needs treatment.
management_principles: Discontinue diuretics and nephrotoxic agents; renal ultrasound and diagnostic paracentesis to exclude structural disease and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Trial of IV albumin (1 g/kg/day for 2 days) plus vasoconstrictor therapy (Terlipressin, or Midodrine + Octreotide + Albumin) to improve renal perfusion
Treat any precipitating infection promptly with empiric antibiotics
Refer urgently for liver transplant evaluation; renal replacement therapy may serve as a bridge
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Hepatorenal Syndrome in Cirrhosis
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for rapidly rising creatinine and oliguria in patient with liver cirrhosis and ascites
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for nephrology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: In decompensated liver cirrhosis, severe splanchnic vasodilation reduces effective blood flow to the kidneys, causing progressive kidney failure that does not improve with fluids or albumin.
differentials: Prerenal AKI from volume depletion (would respond to fluids)
red_flags: Signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever, abdominal pain) — a common trigger that needs treatment

must_ask.say: How long have you had liver cirrhosis, and what caused it?
How has your urine output changed recently?
How has your belly swelling (ascites) changed?
Have you been taking water pills, and has the dose changed recently?

history.answer: My daily urine has dropped to almost nothing over the last couple of weeks, and the clinic told me my kidney numbers are getting dangerously worse.
It has been dwindling steadily for the past two weeks, and now I only pass a tiny trickle maybe twice a day, barely filling half a small cup.
I have been drinking my usual amount of water, and I haven't had any vomiting, diarrhea, excessive sweating, or vomiting blood.
My mouth feels a little dry and I get dizzy whenever I stand up quickly, but I do not feel intensely thirsty.
It is a dark amber color like strong tea, but I have not seen any bright red blood, cola color, or foaming bubbles.
I do not feel pain or burning when I pee, no weak dribble, and my lower belly does not feel painfully full or blocked.
No, I haven't had any pain in my flanks or back, and I have never had kidney stones.
My belly has been very bloated and tight with fluid, and my lower legs are swollen, but I am not short of breath at rest.
My appetite has been poor and my skin feels itchy, but I have not had severe nausea, persistent hiccups, or confusion.
My pulse feels a little fast sometimes, but no irregular fluttering, and I do not have severe muscle weakness.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, skin rashes, joint aches, or coughing up blood.
No, I haven't had a sore throat, runny nose, or skin infection recently.
No unusual muscle soreness, no heavy workouts, and I haven't fallen or suffered any trauma.
No, I have not had any CT scans with contrast dye, angiograms, or recent surgeries.
My stomach is bloated and tight from fluid, but it has not been tender or painful to press on.
I was on water pills for the fluid in my belly, but the doctors stopped them two days ago and gave me albumin IV fluids, which didn't improve my urine.
I have never had any prostate trouble, pelvic cancer, or radiation therapy.
I thought all this fluid swelling up inside my belly was pressing down on my bladder and trapping my urine inside.
I'm scared that my liver has completely given out and that I won't live long enough to walk my daughter down the aisle next month.
I was hoping you could drain this fluid from my stomach with a tap so the pressure comes off and I can pee again.
I have decompensated liver cirrhosis with ascites, but no past history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney trouble.
I was in the hospital recently to have fluid drained from my abdomen, but I have never had any surgeries.
I am not taking any medications at home right now since they stopped my diuretics, and I don't take pain relievers or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I used to drink alcohol socially in the past, but I completely quit drinking after being diagnosed with liver cirrhosis.
I work full-time in an office and live with my wife.
No one in my family has a history of kidney disease or liver conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg, heart rate is 98 beats/min, respiratory rate is 18 breaths/min, and body temperature is 37.0°C.
Conjunctivae are normal without pallor, but sclerae show pronounced icteric discoloration.
Jugular venous pressure is low and not distended.
Breath sounds are vesicular and clear throughout both lung fields without crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Abdomen is prominently distended and tense, with visible spider angiomata across the upper abdomen.
Abdomen is tensely distended but soft, non-tender to light and deep palpation, without rebound tenderness, guarding, or a distended bladder over the suprapubic area.
Marked shifting dullness and a clear fluid wave are present, confirming tense ascites.
No costovertebral angle tenderness is elicited on either side.
Bilateral 2+ pitting edema is noted over the pretibial regions and ankles.
Prominent palmar erythema on both hands and scattered spider nevi over the chest and shoulders, with no petechiae or rash.
Mild asterixis with occasional flapping tremor is observed upon sustained wrist dorsiflexion.
